mcqs.question: What core limitation does long polling still have compared to WebSockets?
options: Long polling still opens a new request for each update, unlike a single persistent WebSocket connection
Long polling cannot deliver updates faster than every 60 seconds
Long polling only works over UDP
Long polling requires no server changes at all
mcqs.explanation: Long polling improves latency over plain polling but still pays the cost of re-establishing a request per update; WebSockets remove that per-message overhead entirely by keeping one connection open. It has no fixed 60-second floor, doesn't require UDP, and does require server-side support to hold requests open.

mcqs.question: Why do WebSocket implementations use ping/pong control frames even when the application has no data to send?
options: To encrypt the connection, since WebSockets have no built-in TLS
To detect a dead connection before intermediate network devices silently time it out
To renegotiate the HTTP upgrade periodically
To compress the data being sent over the connection
mcqs.explanation: Idle connections look identical to dead ones from the network's view; ping/pong lets both sides confirm liveness before a NAT gateway or load balancer silently drops the connection on an idle timeout. It's unrelated to TLS, doesn't re-run the handshake, and isn't a compression mechanism.

mcqs.question: A team wants to push server-generated notifications to the browser one-way — the client never needs to send data back over the same channel. What's a reasonable simpler alternative to WebSockets here?
options: Switching to UDP directly from the browser
There is no simpler alternative to WebSockets for any server push
Server-Sent Events (SSE), since it's built on plain HTTP for one-directional server-to-client streaming
Increasing the polling interval to once per hour
mcqs.explanation: SSE is designed exactly for this shape — server-to-client only, over ordinary HTTP, with built-in browser reconnect — avoiding WebSockets' bidirectional machinery for a need that's actually one-directional. Browsers don't expose raw UDP sockets, and hourly polling would defeat the point of 'real-time.'
